solution.tip: The angle in the formula must be the one between the two given sides ($C$ is between $a$ and $b$).

exercises.questionText: Where appropriate, write angles correct to the nearest minute and other measurements correct to 2 decimal places. Calculate the area of the triangle ABC with $a = 7.3$, $c = 10.8$ and $B = 104^\circ 40'$.

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is approximately 38.14 square units.

exercises.questionText: Where appropriate, write angles correct to the nearest minute and other measurements correct to 2 decimal places. Calculate the area of the triangle ABC with $b = 23.1$, $c = 18.6$ and $A = 82^\circ 17'$.

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is approximately 212.88 square units.
solution.tip: Check your calculator is in degree mode before evaluating the sine.

exercises.questionText: Where appropriate, write angles correct to the nearest minute and other measurements correct to 2 decimal places. A triangle has $a = 10$ cm, $c = 14$ cm and $C = 48^\circ$. Determine $A$ and $B$ and hence the area.

steps: Given: $a = 10$, $c = 14$, $C = 48^\circ$ (not the included angle). Goal: $A$, $B$, area.
$A \approx 32.061^\circ \approx 32^\circ 4'$ (only one triangle since $a < c$ means A must be acute).
B is the angle between $a$ and $c$, so Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 14 \times \sin(99.939^\circ)$
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $A \approx 32^\circ 4'$, $B \approx 99^\circ 56'$ and the area is approximately $68.95\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: When the given angle is not between the given sides, find the included angle first.

exercises.questionText: Where appropriate, write angles correct to the nearest minute and other measurements correct to 2 decimal places. A triangle has $a = 17$ m, $c = 22$ m and $C = 56^\circ$. Determine $A$ and $B$ and hence the area.

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $A \approx 39^\circ 50'$, $B \approx 84^\circ 10'$ and the area is approximately $186.03\text{ m}^2$.
solution.tip: Use the unrounded value of $B$ in the area formula.

exercises.questionText: Where appropriate, write angles correct to the nearest minute and other measurements correct to 2 decimal places. A triangle has $b = 32$ mm, $c = 15$ mm and $B = 38^\circ$. Determine $A$ and $C$ and hence the area.

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $A \approx 125^\circ 14'$, $C \approx 16^\circ 46'$ and the area is approximately $196.05\text{ mm}^2$ (the textbook gives 196.03 mm², which comes from rounding during the working).
solution.tip: Rounding the angle before using it in the area formula changes the second decimal place; keep full calculator values.

exercises.questionText:
MC In a triangle, $a = 15$ m, $b = 20$ m and $B = 50^\circ$. The area of the triangle is:
A. $86.2\text{ m}^2$  B. $114.9\text{ m}^2$  C. $149.4\text{ m}^2$  D. $172.4\text{ m}^2$

solution.formula: Sine rule to find the included angle $C$; area $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin(C)$
solution.tip: Option B is $\frac{1}{2} \times 15 \times 20 \times \sin(50^\circ)$, which wrongly uses an angle that is not between the two sides.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the area of the triangle with sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm (correct to 2 decimal places).

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is approximately $14.98\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: $s$ is half the perimeter, not the full perimeter.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the area of the triangle with sides of 40 mm, 30 mm and 5.7 cm (correct to 2 decimal places).

steps: Given: sides 40 mm, 30 mm and 5.7 cm $= 57$ mm. Goal: area.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is approximately $570.03\text{ mm}^2$.
solution.tip: Convert all sides to the same unit before using Heron's formula.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the area of the triangle with sides of 16 mm, 3 cm and 2.7 cm (correct to 2 decimal places).

steps: Given: 16 mm $= 1.6$ cm, 3 cm and 2.7 cm. Goal: area in cm².
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is approximately $2.15\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: Convert mm to cm by dividing by 10 before you start.

exercises.questionText:
MC A triangle has sides of length 10 cm, 14 cm and 20 cm. The area of the triangle is:
A. $41\text{ cm}^2$  B. $65\text{ cm}^2$  C. $106\text{ cm}^2$  D. $137\text{ cm}^2$

steps: Given: sides 10, 14 and 20 cm. Goal: area.
solution.finalAnswer: B. $65\text{ cm}^2$
solution.tip: Check that each bracket $(s - \text{side})$ is positive; if one is negative the sides cannot form a triangle.

exercises.questionText: A piece of metal is in the shape of a triangle with sides of length 114 mm, 72 mm and 87 mm. Calculate its area (correct to 2 decimal places).

steps: Given: sides 114, 72 and 87 mm. Goal: area.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the metal piece is approximately $3131.41\text{ mm}^2$.
solution.tip: Write out $s - a$, $s - b$, $s - c$ separately before multiplying to avoid slips.

exercises.questionText: A triangle has the largest angle of $115^\circ$. The longest side is 62 cm and another side is 35 cm. Calculate the area of the triangle to the nearest whole number.

steps: Given: $A = 115^\circ$ opposite the longest side $a = 62$ cm; $b = 35$ cm. Goal: area.
$C = 180^\circ - 115^\circ - 30.772^\circ = 34.228^\circ$ (this is the angle between the 62 cm and 35 cm sides).
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the triangle is approximately $610\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: The $115^\circ$ angle is opposite the 62 cm side, so it is not the angle between the two given sides.

exercises.questionText: A triangle has two sides of 25 cm and 30 cm. The angle between the two sides is $30^\circ$. Determine its area.

steps: Given: sides 25 cm and 30 cm, included angle $30^\circ$. Goal: area.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area is $187.5\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: $\sin(30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}$ exactly, so no rounding is needed here.

exercises.questionText: A triangle has two sides of 25 cm and 30 cm. The angle between the two sides is $30^\circ$. Determine the length of its third side (correct to 2 decimal places).

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the third side is approximately 15.03 cm.
solution.tip: Multiply $1500 \times \cos(30^\circ)$ before subtracting from 1525.

exercises.questionText: The surface of a fish pond has the shape shown in the diagram: a quadrilateral with sides 1 m (top), 2 m (left), 4 m (bottom slanted side) and 5 m (right). The 1 m and 2 m sides meet at a right angle. Calculate how many goldfish the pond can support if each fish requires $0.3\text{ m}^2$ surface area of water.

solution.formula: Pythagoras' theorem; cosine rule $\cos(\theta) = \frac{p^2 + q^2 - r^2}{2pq}$; area $= \frac{1}{2}pq\sin(\theta)$
steps: Given: right angle between the 1 m and 2 m sides; other sides 4 m and 5 m. Goal: number of fish.
Draw the diagonal joining the ends of the 1 m and 2 m sides: $d^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 = 5$, so $d = \sqrt{5}$ m.
Other triangle has sides 4, 5 and $\sqrt{5}$. The angle $\theta$ between the 4 m and 5 m sides is opposite $\sqrt{5}$:
Only whole fish, and 18 would need more water than there is, so round down to 17.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the pond can support 17 goldfish.
solution.tip: Round down here: the pond does not have enough surface area for an 18th fish.

exercises.questionText:
MC A parallelogram has sides of 14 cm and 18 cm and an angle between them of $72^\circ$. The area of the parallelogram is:
A. $118.4\text{ cm}^2$  B. $172.4\text{ cm}^2$  C. $239.7\text{ cm}^2$  D. $252\text{ cm}^2$

solution.formula: Parallelogram = 2 congruent triangles, so Area $= 2 \times \frac{1}{2}ab\sin(\theta) = ab\sin(\theta)$
steps: Given: sides 14 cm and 18 cm, angle $72^\circ$. Goal: area.
A diagonal splits the parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
solution.tip: Do not halve for a parallelogram: it is two triangles, not one.

exercises.questionText:
MC An advertising hoarding is in the shape of an isosceles triangle with sides of length 15 m, 15 m and 18 m. It is to be painted with two coats of purple paint. If the paint covers $12\text{ m}^2$ per litre, the amount of paint needed, to the nearest litre, would be:
A. 9 L  B. 18 L  C. 24 L  D. 36 L

steps: Given: sides 15, 15, 18 m; 2 coats; $12\text{ m}^2$ per litre. Goal: litres of paint.
solution.finalAnswer: B. 18 L
solution.tip: Remember to double the area for two coats.

exercises.questionText: A parallelogram has diagonals of length 10 cm and 17 cm. An angle between them is $125^\circ$. Determine the area of the parallelogram (correct to 2 decimal places).

solution.formula: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other; area of each triangle $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin(C)$
steps: Given: diagonals 10 cm and 17 cm meeting at $125^\circ$. Goal: area.
The diagonals bisect each other, so the half-diagonals are 5 cm and 8.5 cm.

The diagonals split the parallelogram into 4 triangles, each with sides 5 and 8.5 and an included angle of $125^\circ$ or $55^\circ$. Since $\sin(125^\circ) = \sin(55^\circ)$, all four have equal area.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the parallelogram is approximately $69.63\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: Use half of each diagonal: the triangles are formed at the point where the diagonals cross.

exercises.questionText: A parallelogram has diagonals of length 10 cm and 17 cm. An angle between them is $125^\circ$. Determine the dimensions of the parallelogram (correct to 2 decimal places).

steps: Given: half-diagonals 5 cm and 8.5 cm; angles between them $125^\circ$ and $180^\circ - 125^\circ = 55^\circ$. Goal: the two side lengths.
Check (parallelogram law, sum of squares of sides equals half the sum of squares of the diagonals): $s_1^2 + s_2^2 = 146.004 + 48.496 = 194.5$ and $\frac{10^2 + 17^2}{2} = 194.5$ ✓
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the parallelogram measures approximately 12.08 cm by 6.96 cm.
solution.tip: The two angles where the diagonals cross are supplementary, giving two different side lengths.

exercises.questionText: A lawn is to be made in the shape of a triangle with sides of length 11 m, 15 m and 17.2 m. Determine how much grass seed, to the nearest kilogram, needs to be purchased if it is sown at the rate of 1 kg per $5\text{ m}^2$.

steps: Given: sides 11, 15 and 17.2 m; 1 kg seed per $5\text{ m}^2$. Goal: kg of seed to buy.
16 kg would not be enough, so round up to the next whole kilogram: 17 kg.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore 17 kg of grass seed needs to be purchased.
solution.tip: When buying materials, round up so there is enough, even if normal rounding would round down.

exercises.questionText: A bushfire burns out an area of level grassland shown in the diagram. (Note: This is a sketch of the area and is not drawn to scale.) The burnt region is a quadrilateral bounded by a road along the bottom (200 m), a river running perpendicular to the road on the right (2 km), a side of 1.8 km from the top of the river side back down-left, and a side of 400 m joining that back to the start of the 200 m road side. There is a right angle between the 200 m road side and the 2 km river side. Evaluate the area, in hectares correct to 1 decimal place, of the land that is burned.

solution.formula: Area of right triangle $= \frac{1}{2}bh$; Heron's formula $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$; $1\text{ km}^2 = 100$ ha
steps: Given: road side 0.2 km, river side 2 km at right angles, other sides 1.8 km and 0.4 km. Goal: area in hectares.
Draw the diagonal from the start of the road side (P) to the top of the river side (T).
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore approximately 52.2 hectares of land is burned.
solution.tip: Convert all lengths to km first, then use $1\text{ km}^2 = 100$ hectares.

exercises.questionText: An earth embankment is 27 m long and has a vertical cross-section as shown in the diagram: a trapezium with a bottom base of 5 m, a left sloping side of 2 m, base angles of $50^\circ$ (left) and $80^\circ$ (right), and top angles of $130^\circ$ (left) and $100^\circ$ (right). Determine the volume of earth needed to build the embankment, correct to the nearest cubic metre.

solution.formula: Height $= 2\sin(50^\circ)$; trapezium area $= \frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$; volume $=$ cross-section area $\times$ length
steps: Given: base 5 m, left side 2 m at $50^\circ$, right side at $80^\circ$, length 27 m. Since $50^\circ + 130^\circ = 180^\circ$, the top is parallel to the base. Goal: volume.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore about $175\text{ m}^3$ of earth is needed.
solution.tip: Find the cross-sectional area first, then multiply by the length of the prism.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate the area of this quadrilateral (correct to 2 decimal places). The quadrilateral has sides 3.5 m (top left), 4 m (left), 5 m (bottom) and 8 m (right, slanted). The angle between the 5 m and 8 m sides is $60^\circ$.

solution.formula: Area $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin(C)$; cosine rule $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos(C)$; Heron's formula
steps: Given: sides 5 m and 8 m with $60^\circ$ between them; sides 3.5 m and 4 m. Goal: total area.
Draw the diagonal joining the free ends of the 5 m and 8 m sides.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the quadrilateral is approximately $22.02\text{ m}^2$.
solution.tip: Split a quadrilateral into two triangles with a diagonal that uses the known angle.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. The side AB could not be measured because it crossed through a marsh. The owner of the property wanted to know the total area and the length of the side AB. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Calculate the area of the triangle ACD.

steps: Given: $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, included angle $D = 60^\circ$. Goal: area of triangle ACD.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of triangle ACD is approximately $29.44\text{ km}^2$.
solution.tip: Angle D is between DC and DA, so it is the included angle.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Calculate the distance AC.

solution.formula: Cosine rule: $AC^2 = DC^2 + DA^2 - 2 \times DC \times DA \cos(D)$
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $AC \approx 8.26$ km.
solution.tip: Keep $AC = \sqrt{68.25}$ in your calculator for later parts.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Calculate the angle CAB.

steps: $\angle CAB \approx 41.16^\circ \approx 41^\circ$ (acute, because the triangle already has an obtuse angle).
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $\angle CAB \approx 41^\circ$.
solution.tip: A triangle can have only one obtuse angle, so there is no ambiguous case here.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Calculate the angle ACB.

solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $\angle ACB \approx 24^\circ$.
solution.tip: Use the unrounded angle from part (c) so later answers stay accurate.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Calculate the length AB.

steps: Check with the cosine rule: $AC^2 = AB^2 + 6^2 - 2(AB)(6)\cos(115^\circ) = 13.569 + 36 + 18.680 = 68.25$ ✓
(If the rounded values $AC = 8.26$ and $\angle ACB = 24^\circ$ are used instead, $AB \approx 3.71$ km.)
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore $AB \approx 3.68$ km (the textbook gives 3.72 km, which comes from using rounded intermediate values).
solution.tip: Rounding angles to the nearest degree before using them can shift a length in the second decimal place.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Determine the area of the triangle ABC.

steps: Given: $AB \approx 3.6836$ km, $CB = 6$ km, included angle $B = 115^\circ$. Goal: area of triangle ABC.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of triangle ABC is approximately $10.02\text{ km}^2$ (the textbook gives 10.11 km², from its rounded AB = 3.72 km).
solution.tip: Use the angle between the two sides you multiply; here $115^\circ$ is between AB and CB.

exercises.questionText: A surveyor measured the boundaries of a property ABCD as shown. $DC = 8$ km, $DA = 8.5$ km, $\angle ADC = 60^\circ$, $CB = 6$ km and $\angle ABC = 115^\circ$. Give all lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles to the nearest degree. Determine the area of the property.

solution.formula: Total area = area of triangle ACD + area of triangle ABC
steps: Given: area ACD $\approx 29.4449\text{ km}^2$, area ABC $\approx 10.0154\text{ km}^2$. Goal: total area.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the property is approximately $39.46\text{ km}^2$ (the textbook gives 39.55 km², carrying its rounded value from part f).
solution.tip: Add the unrounded areas, then round once at the end.

exercises.questionText: A regular hexagon has sides of length 12 centimetres. It is divided into six smaller equilateral triangles. Evaluate the area of the hexagon, giving your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

solution.formula: Area of each equilateral triangle $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin(60^\circ)$; hexagon $= 6 \times$ triangle
steps: Given: side 12 cm; 6 equilateral triangles of side 12 cm with angles of $60^\circ$. Goal: area of the hexagon.
solution.finalAnswer: Therefore the area of the hexagon is approximately $374.12\text{ cm}^2$.
solution.tip: Each angle at the centre of a regular hexagon is $\frac{360^\circ}{6} = 60^\circ$.
